paper_title: Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Low-rank SVD-based compression offers a powerful strategy to reduce the computational costs of LLMs. However, existing methods face two key limitations: (i) global rank allocation, where uncalibrated error proxies fail to capture complex error propagation, and (ii) decomposition quality, where Fisher-based estimators suffer from severe rank collapse. In this work, we address these limitations by introducing Layer-wise Error Modeling Search (LEMS) and KFAC-SVD. LEMS advances rank allocation by introducing a layer-wise error surrogate that integrates local and global layer importance alongside a propagation bias, enabling effective global rank allocation via an ILP formulation. KFAC-SVD improves decomposition quality by utilizing token-wise statistics, mitigating the rank deficiency observed in prior Fisher-based SVD approaches. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3 model families, we show that LEMS consistently outperforms existing search strategies, delivering significant zero-shot accuracy gains of up to 4.7 p.p. that generalize to model sizes of 70B parameters, while KFAC-SVD achieves an average perplexity improvement of 19%. Project page and code: https://lems-svd.github.io

Introduction The rapid scaling of LLMs (Yang et al., 2025; Grattafiori et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023) has enabled previously unattainable capabilities, but introduced substantial computational and memory requirements that limit deployment in resource-constrained environments. To address these lim- *Equal contribution 1Technical University of Munich, Germany 2BMW Group, Germany 3University of Glasgow, United Kingdom 4TU Wien, Austria. By decomposing dense weight matrices into smaller factors, SVD substantially reduces parameter counts and computational complexity while retaining easy-to-accelerate dense tensor computations. This ensures immediate compatibility with standard inference engines, avoiding the specialized hardware or sparse kernels that are often required by semistructured or unstructured pruning approaches. Prior work has demonstrated that SVD-based methods yield significant inference acceleration, particularly in memory-bound regimes, while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art pruning techniques (Qinsi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b;d). They also demonstrate that low-rank approximation is orthogonal to quantization, allowing the two methods to be combined effectively for maximum efficiency. However, the full potential of SVD in modern LLMs is limited by two fundamental challenges: global rank allocation and decomposition quality. The primary bottleneck is the global allocation problem, which requires determining the optimal rank for each layer under fixed parameter budget. Existing strategies fail to solve this optimization effectively, as they rely on uncalibrated local sensitivity proxies (Azizi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b) or expensive measurements (Thoma et al., 2025; Yuan et al., 2024) to determine layer importance. These methods typically neglect the nonlinear error explosion inherent in deep networks (Huang et al., 2025), creating critical misalignment between error proxy and actual degradation. Consequently, their ability to identify high-performance rank allocations remains limited. Further, high decomposition quality requires distinguishing and preserving the weight directions that are most critical for the downstream task. While Fisher-weighted SVD theoretically addresses this by aligning reconstruction error with the loss landscape (curvature), existing work (Chekalina et al., 2025) suffers from rank deficiencies under reasonable sample counts, limiting its effectiveness. In this work, we address both challenges by introducing LEMS for global rank allocation and KFAC-SVD for robust decomposition. LEMS introduces layer-wise error model that integrates local sensitivity, empirical calibraAdvancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search tion, and bias correcting error propagation. By explicitly modeling layer-wise error accumulation, we can formulate the search as an ILP and solve it efficiently. KFAC-SVD mitigates the rank deficiency that limits the decomposition quality of prior Fisher-based SVD by transitioning from sequence-based to token-wise statistics for the Fisher approximation. By accumulating token-level loss curvature information, we effectively prevent rank collapse, yielding decomposition of significantly higher fidelity. Our contributions are threefold: 1. LEMS. We propose layer-wise error model for rank allocation in SVD that captures both local sensitivity and global error propagation modeling error propagation via bias. To obtain global rank allocations we search the error model with an ILP formulation. 2. Robust Fisher Decomposition (KFAC-SVD). We leverage token-wise Kronecker-factor estimation in SVD to mitigate the rank bottleneck of prior Fisherbased SVD and improve its decomposition quality. 3. Empirical Validation. Across Mistral, Qwen3, and Llama 3, KFAC-SVD improves WikiText2 perplexity by an average of 19% over baselines. LEMS further drives substantial accuracy gains of 2.1-4.7 p.p. compared to the best existing rank allocation methods. Crucially, it also generalizes to activation-based SVD and scales to the 70B parameter regime, achieving 4.0 p.p. improvement over uniform rank allocation. 2. Related Work Low Rank Decomposition. Standard SVD compression replaces weight, W, with rank-r approximation, Wr, that minimizes WrF . This is optimal for weight reconstruction, but often suboptimal for model performance, as deviation magnitude is poor proxy for importance. To better match the forward computation, recent methods optimize an activation-based objective, targeting the layeroutput error WX WrXF . ASVD (Yuan et al., 2024) weights the rows of the weight matrices by activation importance. Building on this idea, SVD-LLM (Wang et al., 2025d) demonstrates that whitening using Cholesky factor of the input activation covariance yields the optimal rank-r approximation for minimizing the Frobenius layer-output error. Subsequent work improves numerical stability (Wang et al., 2025b) and estimation accuracy of the covariance (Thoma et al., 2025) while keeping the same output-reconstruction objective. Basis-Sharing (Wang et al., 2025a) builds on SVD-LLM but reuses low-rank bases across layers to reduce parameters on disk, creating unique memory-computation trade-offs. DOBI-SVD (Qinsi et al., 2025) departs from direct weight whitening by truncating activations and fitting low-rank weights that best preserve the retained features: Because activations are modified during the forward pass, the effective objective differs slightly from SVD-LLM-style methods. It also introduces remapping, which is essentially quantization of decomposed components. BitStack (Wang et al., 2025c) fundamentally alters the decomposition process, separating it from prior SVD-based methods. While activation-based methods effectively preserve feature representations, complementary research targets the loss landscape directly. These methods model compression impact via local second-order (Taylor) approximation, yielding Fisher-weighted objectives. Fisher-weighted SVD (Hsu et al., 2022) uses diagonal Fisher approximation to weight truncation by parameter importance, while GFWSVD (Chekalina et al., 2025) improves curvature modeling using Kronecker-factored Fisher, demonstrating that two-sided whitening yields the optimal rank-r solution under this approximation. Our approach. Activation-based methods are robust but loss-agnostic, whereas Fisher-weighted compression is lossaware. Current Fisher-based work relies on sequencegradient fitting, sample-limited at LLM scale. To mitigate, we estimate Kronecker factors from token-wise second moments, making truncation viable and stable in large models. Searching for Ranks. Assigning different ranks to different layers can substantially improve quality at fixed compression budget (Yuan et al., 2024; Thoma et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Azizi et al., 2025). Existing approaches primarily differ in their search and optimization strategies. (i) Greedy rank allocation. Several methods use greedy procedures that progressively increase compression while tracking reconstruction metrics. Both MRCS (Azizi et al., 2025) and FastLRD (Luo et al., 2024) iteratively adjust ranks to control energy loss or weight-based similarity, aiming to keep layer-wise reconstruction error small. (ii) Balanced reconstruction error. commonly adopted heuristic allocates compression across layers to achieve similar reconstruction errors. ASVD evaluates candidate layer-wise configurations and applies binary search to find uniform error threshold that satisfies global budget. Flar-SVD (Thoma et al., 2025) performs per-layer binary searches to more precisely equalize reconstruction error in vision transformers, while SVD-LLMv2 (Wang et al., 2025b) groups weights by type (attention vs. MLP) and redistributes compression within each group based on relative loss contributions inferred from removed singular values. (iii) Learned rank allocation. further class of methods learns rank importance directly. ComCat (Xiao et al., 2023) introduces trainable signals for per-layer rank allocation, while ARS (Gao et al., 2024b) and the search component of DOBI-SVD (Qinsi et al., 2025) optimize ranks via gradientupdated masks that are controlled by small hyper-network. Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search (iv) Further sparsity allocation. Related search problems appear in structured and semi-structured pruning. MDP (Sun et al., 2025) formulates structured sparsity allocation as an ILP, enabling one-shot global optimization. ATP (Huang et al., 2025) analyzes error propagation and shows that lower bounds on reconstruction error increase for later layers when early layers are compressed, motivating simple linear allocation scheme that increases compression depth-wise. Our approach. Current rank-search methods often (i) rely on greedy updates with limited global optimality guarantees, (ii) target uniform error distributions rather than minimizing total error, or (iii) require gradient-based optimization with tuned hyper parameters. Inspired by ILP-based sparsity allocation (Sun et al., 2025) and propagation analyses (Huang et al., 2025), we propose to directly minimize total error under global budget by solving an ILP over discrete perlayer rank candidates using layer-wise proxy model. Concurrent work. Work concurrently released to ours, such as OBD-LLM (Li et al., 2026), IO-SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026a), ZS-SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026b) and Swift-SVD (Qi et al., 2026) is discussed and evaluated in Section B.5. 3. Effective rank allocation requires accurately predicting the contribution of given rank choice, ri, for linear layer weight, e.g., WQ, Wdown, to the global model degradation. This problem poses three distinct challenges: 1. Granularity (Shape): Solving the allocation problem requires loss estimators for all candidate ranks across weights; however, evaluating these via forward passes is computationally intractable. 2. Sensitivity (Scale): Standard proxies derived from SVD spectra, e.g., tail energy, are informative but uncalibrated. 10% spectral energy loss in MLP projection may impact the output differently than 10% loss in an attention projection (see Figure 1b). 3. Propagation (Bias): Losses are not strictly additive. Errors introduced in early layers propagate and amplify through the depth of the network. Simply summing layer-wise errors systematically underestimates global degradation for compressed models (see Figure 1c). Existing approaches fail to address these challenges simultaneously. Methods relying on spectral energy (Wang et al., 2025b; Azizi et al., 2025) are uncalibrated (sensitivity) and ignore propagation. Similarly, measurement approaches (Yuan et al., 2024; Thoma et al., 2025) are not only intractable for fine-grained search (granularity) but also fail to model propagation. The only exception addressing propagation, (Huang et al., 2025), sacrifices sensitivity by enforcing uniform block-wise compression rates. Method. To systematically address these challenges, we rely on two core components: (i) decomposable cost model that disentangles complex loss contributions via spectral shape (for granularity), calibration point (for scale), and depth-dependent bias (for propagation); and (ii) an ILP that identifies the globally optimal allocation under this proxy. This enables rank selection to be formulated as constrained combinatorial optimization problem over the set of linear layers, = {W1, ..., WNL}, distributed across transformer blocks. Additional results, evaluation and further information are available in the supplementary material. Models, Baselines and Datasets. We compare LEMS to variation of searches. Implementation Details. To ensure fair comparison, all methods are tested under identical settings (incl. seed). For calibration of SVD algorithms, we use 256 random sequences of length 2048 from WikiText2. For search methods involving data, we use 32 samples from WikiText2 following ASVD. For the ILP search we use the Gurobi solver (Gurobi Optimization, LLC, 2024), with per layer search range of ci = [0.3, 1.0]. Compression ratios refer to the remaining parameters of linear layers (excluding head). All experiments are run on single NVIDIA H200 GPU. Additional Results. For detailed tables, data ablations, more architectures and results on non-standard SVD (i.e. BasisSharing, BitStack) we refer to the Supplement. 5.1. Rank Allocation Results We evaluate the proposed LEMS rank allocation against representative searches. All methods employ the same decomposition pipeline, calibration data and candidate ranks, differing only in rank selection (refer to Supplement A). We report perplexity on WikiText2, C4 and PTB (lower is better), and average zero-shot accuracy (higher is better) for two compression ratios (0.8, 0.6) across three architectures  (Table 1)  . Per-task accuracies are provided in Supplement D. Uniform search: Across all six settings, LEMS achieves the highest accuracy and substantially reduces perplexity relative to uniform rank allocation. The accuracy gain over the second-best method ranges from 2.14 to 4.67 percentage points (p.p.) while the (mean) perplexity averaged over WikiText2, C4 and PTB is reduced, relative to uniform allocation, by 26.06 to 75.40%. Baseline searches: Among the baselines, ASVD and SVD-LLMv2 frequently fail to outperform uniform allocation, consistent with the limitations of noisy, sensitivity proxies (cf. Supplement B.1.2) and constraints that enforce overly similar compression across heterogeneous layer types (cf. Supplement B.1.3), respectively. Similarly, MRCS struggles in most settings. ARS is the strongest baseline in accuracy, ranking second in four of the six settings. However, its WikiText2 perplexity is worse than uniform allocation in four of the six settings, and it requires gradients, more data, and stabilized schedule to reliably meet target ratios. Despite its simplicity, ATP, which is the only baseline explicitly modeling accumulating errors, generally matches or narrowly outperforms uniform allocation and remains competitive with other searches, especially on Llama 3. However, because it assumes error accumulation as linear function, it cannot capture layerand type-specific importance deviations. Overall, the results strongly validate the efficacy of LEMS. 5.2. LEMS demonstrates consistent gains independent of model size and across activationand Fisher-based SVD. Additionally, we addressed the rank bottleneck of prior Fisherbased SVD by introducing KFAC-SVD, which estimates the Fisher matrix with token-wise approximation, improving decomposition quality. While improving Fisher-SVD, our proposed KFAC-SVD approach still relies on gradient computation, limiting computational efficiency. Moreover, LEMS relies on one-time layer-wise calibration step, which scales linearly with model depth. All models were sourced from HuggingFace, utilizing optimized implementations from Unsloth where available. For the Qwen3 Family, we utilize the official checkpoints for the entire scaling suite, specifically Qwen/Qwen3-32B, -14B, -8B, -4B, and -1.7B (Yang et al., 2025). For the Llama 3 Family, we evaluate Llama 3 , the very large Llama 3.1 (70B) and the lightweight Llama 3.2 variants (1B, 3B) (Grattafiori et al., 2024), alongside the established Llama 2-7B (Touvron et al., 2023b), using the unrestricted Unsloth-optimized versions (e.g., unsloth/llama-3-8b). Finally, for Mistral, we evaluate the Mistral-7B-v0.1 model (Jiang et al., 2023) via unsloth/mistral-7b. Search Baselines and Implementation Details. To ensure fair comparison, all search methods utilize the same decomposition approach and candidate rank sets where applicable. We implemented or adapted the baselines as follows: Activation-aware singular value decomposition (ASVD) (Yuan et al., 2024): We utilize the official public codebase with default settings as reference, where the search evaluates sensitivity on the calibration set to select ranks from discrete set of multipliers. Mixed rank compression strategy (MRCS) (Azizi et al., 2025): As no official code was available, we reimplemented the algorithm following the published methodology. Following their setup, we set the sensitivity parameter γ = 80 and limit the search to 500 iterations. To maintain valid search space comparable to other methods, we lower-bound the compression ratio per layer at ci = 0.3. Optimizing SVD for LLM compression (SVD-LLMv2) (Wang et al., 2025b): We re-implemented the search algorithm based on the paper description, as the code remains unavailable. Adaptive rank selection (ARS) (Gao et al., 2024b): We used the public ARS implementation (https://github. com/sidhantls/adaptive-rank-selection-svd) with three crucial modifications to ensure fair benchmarking. First, we initialize the model with our pre-computed singular value decomposition (SVD) factors rather than using their decomposition implementation to isolate the benefit of the search algorithm. Second, we aligned their parameter counting and compression ratio logic with our framework to ensure all methods target the exact same parameter budget. Third, we adjusted the training schedule, because the default values resulted in severe overcompression. With the adjustment, once the ratio is within 0.2% of the target retention, the compression loss is disabled and the alignment loss is scaled by 0.1. For hyperparameters, we used the default settings for Llama 3-8B across all models (γ = 1 for Mistral-7B at 0.6). In our tests, ARS typically converges within 200 iterations using about 7 the data of ASVD and LEMS. theoretical perspective (on sparsity) (ATP) (Huang et al., 2025): We execute the grid search procedure as specified in the original paper. We perform 10 grid-search steps over the valid linearly space and report the best performing configuration. LEMS (Proposed): For our method, we use the Optuna framework (Akiba et al., 2019) to fit the bias parameters. To maintain computational parity with ATP, we limit the optimization to 10 trials. The search space for the bias magnitude is bounded to κ [0.0, 3.0] and the decay shape to γ (0.0, 7.0). For the scale calibration, we measure the Kullback-Leibler divergence (KL) sensitivity at reference compression of cref = 0.1, as the signal-to-noise ratio of the relative importance is larger under strong compression. Finally, we constrain the layer-wise compression range to match ASVD. Additional details on our methods design choices and the algorithm are provided in the supplementary Section B.1 and C, respectively. B. Additional Ablations B.1. Extended Explanations and Ablations for LEMS This section provides empirical validation for the design choices of our LEMS algorithm. We first investigate the necessity of the bias term by quantifying error propagation in Supplement B.1.1. We then analyze the scale component in Supplement B.1.2, comparing different importance metrics and calibration points to identify the most robust signal for global Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search rank allocation. Next, we provide detailed comparison between LEMS, ATP, and ASVD in Section B.1.3. Finally, in Section B.1.4 we discuss how the individual components of LEMS contribute to its performance and how the combination of the components allows surpassing prior works. B.1.1. BIAS FUNCTION IN ERROR MODELING Theoretical Justification. The necessity of depth-dependent bias term is grounded in the theoretical analysis of error propagation. Recent work by Huang et al. (2025) formalizes the concept of Reconstruction Error Explosion (Theorem 3.2), proving that in simplified linear network, increasing the error in layer strictly increases the lower bound of the error in layer + 1: L(Wi+1, Xi+1) > σ2 min( (cid:102)Wi+1) L(Wi, Xi). (16) This inequality implies cascade effect where early-layer errors are amplified by the singular values of all subsequent layers. However, this theoretical bound assumes strictly linear feed-forward structure. Modern LLMs introduce complex non-linearities (e.g., SwiGLU), normalizations (RMSNorm), and crucial residual connections that dampen or distort this propagation in ways that are analytically highly difficult to model precisely. Consequently, while theory confirms that an error penalty must exist and should be higher for initial layers, deriving its exact analytical form is unfeasible for Transformers. We therefore adopt hybrid approach: we accept the theoretical mandate for depth-dependent penalty but determine its specific shape and magnitude empirically. Our bias term β(di) is thus parameterized correction that adapts the theoretical error explosion principle to the empirical reality of residual-heavy LLM architectures. Quantifying Error Underestimation. To verify that this theoretical error accumulation manifests in practice, despite the mitigating effects of residual connections and norm layers, we perform sequential compression experiment. We first measure the error induced by compressing each block di {1, ..., B} individually. We then compress the model cumulatively from the last block to the first, measuring the actual, total degradation at each step. Figure 5 compares the naive sum of individual errors against the measured total error. The results confirm systematic underestimation: as more blocks are compressed, the true error diverges from the additive proxy. This divergence is particularly pronounced in the Llama 3.2-3B model, where early perturbations amplify significantly as they propagate. In Qwen3-4B, while the additive approximation holds better, the underestimation remains present. This confirms that simply minimizing local errors is insufficient. Hence, we find that the optimization objective needs to be corrected with depth-dependent bias β(di) to approximate the true upper bound of the loss. Determining Bias Parameters in Practice. Since the exact magnitude of error propagation depends on architecture depth and residual structure, the optimal bias parameters, κ and γ, cannot be fixed universally. To determine them efficiently, we implement lightweight hyperparameter search using the Tree-structured parzen estimation (TPE) algorithm provided by Optuna (Akiba et al., 2019). The process is formulated as bilevel optimization: in the outer loop, the TPE sampler suggests candidate values for κ and γ. In the inner loop, we (1) update the cost function Li(c) with these parameters, (2) solve the integer linear program (ILP) to obtain the optimal rank configuration, (3) temporarily compress the model to these ranks, and (4) measure the KL divergence on small calibration set. Because the ILP solver is extremely fast ( 1s) and we utilize precomputed outputs for the uncompressed model, this entire loop is computationally inexpensive. We run 10 trials, which complete in minutes on single GPU, yielding fitted error propagation model that is calibrated to the specific target model and compression budget. Discussion - Optimization formulation. We note that our interaction correction term, β(di, κ, γ), admits two complementary interpretations: (i) as calibrated reweighting of the per-module surrogate costs, and (ii) as an implicit mechanism for enforcing depth-wise structural prior supported by theory and prior empirical findings. 16 Advancing SVD-based LLM Compression via Layer-Wise Error Model Search classical Lagrangian formulation would operationalize this explicitly by introducing constraint on depth-weighted compression (or degradation) in early blocks and associating multiplier λ that quantifies the cost of violating this prior, formalizing surrogate Lagrangian relaxation (Bragin et al., 2015). In practice, we instead fit κ and γ via lightweight bilevel loop that directly optimizes the ground-truth proxy metric (KL on small calibration set). This approach is more robust in the discrete ILP setting: small dual-ascent updates of κ can induce abrupt jumps in the rank allocation, and hand-specifying constraint threshold is modeland budget-dependent. Our TPE-based calibration avoids these issues while operationalizing the same prior, selecting bias parameters that best align the ILP solution with observed KL behavior. Conceptually, the Lagrangian perspective remains useful: κ can be interpreted as an implicit shadow price on early-block compression, and extending the method to additional depth-wise structural constraints (e.g., monotonicity or smoothness across blocks) naturally corresponds to introducing additional multipliers. Future work could explore surrogateor levelbased Lagrangian relaxations in the ILP to tighten the relaxation and further improve rank allocation search efficiency and performance (Bragin et al., 2015; Bessa et al., 2025). B.1.2. CORRECT CROSS-LAYER SCALING (IMPORTANCE) The Need for Calibrated Importance. To allocate ranks optimally, the search algorithm must weigh the cost of compressing an multi-layer perceptron (MLP) projection layer in the first block of model against an Attention projection layer near the model output. This requires global importance metric. If the proxy objective wrongly assumes one layer-type is easier to compress than another, the ILP solver will aggressively truncate the sensitive layer, degrading performance. Challenges in Importance Estimation. Accurate sensitivity analysis is computationally expensive. Llama 3-8B has 32 blocks with 7 linear layers each, which in turn have hundreds or even thousands of valid rank options, making the evaluation of every rank configuration intractable. Existing solutions fall into two camps: 1. Calibration-based (e.g., ASVD (Yuan et al., 2024)): Measures empirical loss on validation set. While accurate, it is costly (hours per model) and sparse (checking only few discrete ranks), often missing the optimal operating point. 2. Energy-based (e.g., SVD-LLMv2 and MRCS (Wang et al., 2025b; Azizi et al., 2025)): Uses the Frobenius norm of discarded weights (or activations). DETAILED COMPARISON BETWEEN LEMS, ATP AND ASVD This section provides detailed analysis of our pruning search strategy against two leading competitors, ATP and ASVD. To isolate the differences in their allocation strategies, we configure all methods to target 80% parameter retention on the Llama 3.2-3B model. For ASVD, we leverage our more accurate error model (without bias) to ensure the comparison focuses strictly on the search algorithms efficacy. An effective compression strategy must account for the heterogeneous importance of different model components. As illustrated in Figure 9, the relative importance of layers in both Llama 3.2-3B and Qwen3-4B is highly non-uniform. This variation exists across block positions/depth (Figure 9, left plots) and is especially pronounced across different layer types (Figure 9, right plots). For instance, the feed-forward layers (up-proj, down-proj) are substantially more critical than the attention projection layers (q-proj, k-proj). The primary limitation of existing methods lies in how they address this heterogeneity. ATP simply employs monotonically increasing compression ratio across blocks. As seen in Figure 10 (middle), this approach disregards the nuanced importance landscape, resulting in uniform compression across all block layer types. This indiscriminate compression leads to suboptimal performance (13.48 perplexity) due to over compression of critical layers. ASVD represents an improvement by considering layer-specific importance, achieving better perplexity of 12.06. Its compression profile is more varied than ATPs (Figure 10, bottom). However, ASVDs greedy, layer-by-layer optimization aiming towards most equal error fails to capture the global picture. While it correctly preserves more parameters in important layer types, its allocation is not as finely tuned as our LEMS, leading to less efficient parameter-performance trade-offs. In contrast, our global search strategy excels by finding an optimal configuration for the given error model. Comparison with Concurrent Work Multiple SVD works have been proposed simultaneously to the original submission of this work and its final publication. To explore the capabilities of these related works, we extend our analysis with the four most related methods. Similar to our KFAC-SVD, both OBD-LLM (Li et al., 2026) and IO-SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026a) rely on double sided whitening, while ZS-SVD (Abbasi et al., 2026b) and Swift-SVD (Qi et al., 2026) propose new rank allocation strategy concurrent to LEMS. We reimplemented all methods based on their public code or formal algorithm and verified the implementation against the Llama-7B or Llama2-7B results originally reported in the respetive publication. Double-sided decompositions. OBD-LLM takes principled approach that derives the decomposition from Kronecker factorization of the layer Hessian. Since it also relies on the same KFAC Fisher approximation as KFAC-SVD it is very close to our work. The main practical difference is the factor damping. OBD-LLM damps the factors of both sides by 0.1 times their mean diagonal, whereas KFAC-SVD shrinks both factors towards scaled identity (Algorithm 2), with strength of 0.1 on the input and 0.3 on the output side. IO-SVD is also close and, again, uses the same input factor as OBD-LLM and KFAC-SVD. However, for the output factor it uses KL divergence over the top-K next-token probabilities to obtain second-order expansion for the factor. The number of top-k values, that are considered in the expansion varies with the compression ratio (K = 5 at 0.8, = 4 at 0.6). Notably, IO-SVD is more expensive than OBD-LLM and KFAC-SVD as it requires backward passes for its construction rather than just one. Since IO-SVDs code is not currently public, we reimplemented it based on the paper. However, as its damping and probe construction are not fully disclosed, we cannot recover their results exactly. In our testing, for example, top-K of = 8 works better than the = 5 (0.8) and = 4 (0.6) selected in the paper, so we use = 8 throughout. On Llama-7B, our IO-SVD implementation achieves WikiText2 perplexity of 7.41 / 11.45 (reference: 7.31 / 11.20), for 0.8 and 0.6 retention, respectively. sections.content: 59.93 60.83 B.7.1. BITSTACK BitStack Differences to Standard SVD. BitStack (Wang et al., 2025c) uses fundamentally different approach to standard low-rank decomposition of weights. Specifically, they iteratively separate the sign out of the weight matrix resulting in , decompose it to SVD(W ), truncate the result to rank k=16 and reconstruct it to k. Subsequently, they compute the difference of the reconstructed and the original weight and separate sign and decompose the difference again. This way, with an increasing number of iterative steps, their weight approximation becomes better and better. As shown in Wang et al. (2025c) , this method is highly effective, preserving perplexity and zero shot accuracy well, even at low memory footprints. However, there are two main drawbacks: first, the approach is reconstructing the full weight before the forward pass, which makes it computationally expensive and results in slowdowns compared to the baseline, even with highly optimized kernels. In their paper they report it to be about 10% slower than the fp16 baseline at approximately 25% remaining size; second, separating out the binary mask makes combining it with quantization ineffective, specifically, in every iterative step binary tensor with the size of the original weight is extracted. Hence, when using only 4 iterative steps, which is very few already, the binary masks alone take up the same amount of space as the original weight when quantized to 4 bit (excluding scaling factors). While the decomposed weight also contributes to the memory footprint and is quantizable, the space occupied by the non-quantizable binary mask is significantly larger. Hence, different to other SVD approaches, applying quantization to BitStack has negligible memory advantages. Looking at Llama 3-8b example, the proj layer has shape of 4096 4096. With just 4 iterative blocks BitStack uses 4096 4096 4 1 bit = 67, 108, 864 for the sign mask, while using 16 ranks for each of the 4 blocks for the decomposed weight results in (4096 4 16 + 4096 4 16) 16 bit = 8, 388, 608 bit. In total this makes 75, 497, 472 bit, which is 28.125% of the original weight. Now, when considering 4 bit quantization with 128 group size, the total bit count for the decomposed part comes down from 8, 388, 608 to 2, 162, 688 bit. Considering this quantization, the total comes down to 25.81% of the original weight size. Meanwhile, when considering the same weight compressed with other SVD methods and combined with quantization, all layer components are quantizable. Hence, when performing mild SVD compression that removes only 10% of parameters and perform 4 bit quantization on top of it, we get (4096 1844 + 1844 4096) 16 bit = 241, 696, 768 bit for the decomposition, and 62, 312, 448 bit when quantizing to 128 groups 4 bit, reducing it to 23.21% of the original size. Hence, the total reduction achieved when combining it with quantization is similar while likely achieving runtime acceleration. Therefore, overall, combining traditional SVD with quantization is more effective as it allows for inference acceleration and high weight reduction, which BitStacks sign separation approach cannot offer. BitStack Performance Evaluation. In this section, we compare KFAC-SVD with BitStack (Wang et al., 2025c), which we treat separately due to its fundamentally different decomposition. Unlike the other SVD-based methods evaluated so far, which preserve separate low-rank layers at inference time (Equation (5)), BitStack requires reconstructing full weights prior to computation with limited quantization impact as described above. In Table 13, we compare the memoryaccuracy trade-off on Llama 3-8B, as provided in the BitStack repository. To reflect realistic deployment, we report performance under AWQ quantization for both methods. For BitStack, however, we only report the theoretical footprint under AWQ without actually compressing it, since its low-rank structure is incompatible with standard quantization kernels. Even under this favorable assumption for the baseline, our decomposition and search yield better trade-off, improving compression while maintaining higher accuracy. B.7.2. Calibration Data Ablations Since our method uses data-based calibration, we investigate the impact the data has on the final result. For that we investigate the impact of the sample count, the sample seed and the dataset. Impact of Sample Count. We start with investigating the sample count. In Figure 11 (left), the performance improves when more samples become available, as one would expect. Going from 64 to 512 (8) samples, perplexity improves from 20.54 to 17.54, with diminishing returns: doubling from 64 to 128 samples gains 1.98, doubling from 256 (our default) to 512 only 0.46. Impact of Random Seed. We continue with the evaluation of the random seed (Figure 11, right). The seed has smaller impact than the sample count, with the largest difference being 1.05 perplexity (between seed 0 and seed 42). Impact of Calibration Dataset. In all experiments, we used the WikiText2 dataset for calibration. To understand the impact of the calibration set, we repeated the experiments for the 7B and 8B models using the fineweb 16M dataset introduced by (Penedo et al., 2024). This dataset was chosen for its diversity and absence from most common comparisons, allowing for an unbiased evaluation. The results are given in Table 16. When comparing the results to the WikiText2 calibration, it is clear that the calibration set has significant impact on the performance of all methods. While the WikiText2 performance, as expected, drops significantly, PTB, C4 and the classification task performance improve. Specifically, for our method at 0.7 compression, on Llama 3-8B the accuracy improves from 43.69 to 45.19 without search and from 49.88 to 51.18 with search. Similarly, the performance improves from 46.26 to 46.87 without and from 51.68 to 52.61 with search for Mistral-7B and from 48.24 to 50.86 without and from 53.30 to 54.89 with search for Qwen3-8B, experiencing the biggest improvement. Other methods see comparable improvements e.g. SVD-LLM which improves by 1.07 p.p. and 1.93 p.p. for 0.7 and 0.9 on Qwen3-8B, respectively.
